categories.description_en: Tasks a professional is paid for: legal analysis, finance and tax questions, office documents, spreadsheets, research memos and other desk work. The tests here hand the model a realistic brief and judge the finished product, often with a human expert or an expert-written rubric.
categories.description_ru: Право, финансы, налоги, офисные документы, аналитика и другие профессиональные задачи.

categories.description_en: Changing and repairing real programs. The model works inside a repository or a terminal over many steps, reads the code, runs commands, and is scored on whether the resulting change passes hidden tests or a reviewer. This is the busiest category on every launch page.
categories.description_ru: Изменение и восстановление реальных программ, работа с репозиториями, терминалом и многошаговые задачи разработки.

categories.description_en: Training and improving models rather than ordinary software: reproducing a research paper, running an experiment, tuning a training recipe, writing a compute kernel. The score is usually whether the resulting artifact works or reaches a target.
categories.description_ru: Обучение и улучшение моделей, воспроизведение ML-исследований, экспериментирование и вычислительные ядра.

categories.description_en: Mathematics from contest problems to research-level questions, plus scientific reasoning and laboratory knowledge in chemistry, physics and biology. Dangerous biological capabilities are kept out of this category and sit under Biosecurity.
categories.description_ru: Математические задачи, научное рассуждение, лабораторные знания и научные исследования; биологические риски выделены отдельно.

categories.description_en: Finding, matching and using information spread across very long inputs: hundreds of thousands or a million tokens of documents, transcripts or structured data. The tests plant facts or relationships deep in the input and check whether the model can still use them.
categories.description_ru: Извлечение, сопоставление и использование информации в длинных документах и контексте.

categories.description_en: Operating a computer the way a person does: a desktop, a browser, a mobile device, through screenshots and clicks rather than an API. Tasks are everyday chores in real applications, scored on whether the end state is correct. Open-ended web research has its own category.
categories.description_ru: Управление интерфейсами настольных приложений, сайтов и устройств; самостоятельный поиск знаний выделен отдельно.

categories.description_en: Images, charts, video, audio, scanned documents and sheet music, and reasoning that connects them with text. The model has to read what it sees or hears and answer about it.
categories.description_ru: Изображения, графики, видео, аудио, документы и связи между модальностями.

categories.description_en: Finding and fixing vulnerabilities, reproducing known flaws in controlled test environments, analysing binaries and operating production systems under failure. These tests measure capability in a sandbox; the safety category measures whether the model refuses to misuse it.
categories.description_ru: Поиск и исправление уязвимостей, эксплуатация в оценочных средах, анализ и обратная разработка программ.

categories.description_en: Broad knowledge, logic and abstract problem solving, factual accuracy and the mixed question sets that try to cover everything at once. The benchmarks here are the ones most often quoted as a single headline number.
categories.description_ru: Общая эрудиция, логика, абстрактные задачи, фактическая корректность и смешанные наборы способностей.

categories.description_en: Writing code from a specification without a long agentic process: a function, a component, a drawing, an algorithm. Scored by tests, by rendering the output, or by a judge comparing candidates.
categories.description_ru: Программирование по условию, алгоритмические задачи и локальная генерация кода без обязательного длительного агентного процесса.

categories.description_en: Calling functions and APIs, chaining tools, planning multi-step work and carrying a long task to the end. The environments range from office automation to games, and the score is whether the whole workflow completed.
categories.description_ru: Вызовы функций и API, координация инструментов, планирование и длительные агентные задачи, включая игры.

categories.description_en: Finding hard-to-locate facts on the open web and synthesising an answer from many pages. The questions are built so that no single page answers them.
categories.description_ru: Поиск фактов, глубокое исследование и синтез сведений из веб-источников.

categories.description_en: Obeying constraints: output formats, length limits, data schemas, forbidden words and multi-step user requirements. The score is how many constraints the answer honoured.
categories.description_ru: Соблюдение ограничений, форматов, схем данных и многошаговых пользовательских требований.

categories.description_en: Knowledge and task performance across natural languages other than English. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
categories.description_ru: Знания и выполнение задач на разных естественных языках.

categories.description_en: Creative and editorial writing, style, role play, and the emotional and social quality of a conversation. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
categories.description_ru: Творческие и редакционные тексты, стиль, ролевые диалоги, эмоциональные и социальные навыки.

categories.description_en: Clinical and medical knowledge, medical documents, and the quality and safety of help given in a medical conversation, usually graded against rubrics written by physicians.
categories.description_ru: Клинические и медицинские знания, медицинские документы и качество помощи в медицинских диалогах.

categories.description_en: Tests of dangerous biological capability and of dual-use risk: virology know-how, wet-lab troubleshooting, and whether the model refuses requests that could help build a weapon. Some sets also cover chemical and cyber risk. Here a high capability score is not good news, and the refusal scores are the ones to read.
categories.description_ru: Оценки опасных биологических возможностей и риска двойного применения; некоторые наборы дополнительно включают химические и киберриски.

categories.description_en: Refusals of harmful requests, resistance to jailbreaks, honesty under pressure, sycophancy, and whether an agent discloses its own failures or takes forbidden shortcuts. Most of these are rates where lower is better; the table says so on each row.
categories.description_ru: Отказы, вредные инструкции, обход защит, честность поведения, подхалимство и другие оценки безопасного поведения.

categories.description_en: CAD modelling, electrical engineering, spatial design and the production of engineering artifacts from a specification, scored on whether the artifact meets the spec.
categories.description_ru: CAD, электротехника, пространственное проектирование и создание инженерных артефактов.

categories.description_en: Head-to-head preference rankings by people or judge models, and composite indexes that average many unrelated tests into one number. A specialised index stays in its own category; only the catch-all ones live here.
categories.description_ru: Общие рейтинги по предпочтениям людей или судей и сводные индексы нескольких разных направлений. Специализированные индексы остаются в своём направлении.

about.notes: The evaluation page gives version v1.1 but no launch date. The 'printed by Anthropic' label comes from the aggregator and was not confirmed here. Third-party mirrors (BenchLM) show scores that conflict with the Artificial Analysis page, so use the primary page for figures.
about.what_it_tests: AA-Briefcase tests AI agents on long, multi-week business projects in fields such as data science, product management and corporate strategy. The material is four multi-week projects with thousands of input files and 91 tasks in total, and each task asks for a professional deliverable such as a spreadsheet, presentation or memo. Each deliverable is graded on pass-or-fail rubric checks plus pairwise comparisons for analytical quality and presentation, and these are combined into an Elo score. The evaluation is private and run by Artificial Analysis.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

about.maintainer: UC Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (rdi-berkeley), with Snorkel AI hosting the leaderboard and contributing task work and funding. Paper: arXiv 2606.05405; code: github.com/rdi-berkeley/agents-last-exam; Snorkel lists a release date of 2026-06-09. Printed labels say Google, OpenAI and Alibaba; no source found connects those companies to the benchmark, so those attributions are unconfirmed. Aggregator pass-rate figures conflict and are not used.
about.what_it_tests: Agents' Last Exam tests AI agents on long, realistic professional tasks with checkable outcomes, covering 55 sub-industries of the non-physical economy. Agents get only a task description and work in full operating-system sandboxes, and outputs are graded against hidden, deterministic reference answers. The public release (ALE-V1) has 147 tasks drawn from a larger corpus of more than 1,500.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Android team) for the Android Bench of that name; the Alibaba-printed AndroidBench label is not confirmed as the same benchmark. The Google blog was not fetched (a redirect to a Google sorry page blocked it), so the description rests on search snippets and secondary coverage. The Alibaba-printed AndroidBench listing (Qwen3.8 Max at 0.751 on llm-stats) is a different entry and could not be matched to any source. Google's benchmark has been the closest name match, but the family may not be the same test.
about.what_it_tests: Google's Android Bench measures how well AI models handle Android app development tasks, using a curated set of real open-source Android projects. A patch counts as correct when it passes that project's test suite. Google later moved the benchmark onto the Harbor agent sandbox framework and added models to its leaderboard.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: created by François Chollet; co-founded by Mike Knoop. The foundational paper is François Chollet's 'On the measure of intelligence' (arXiv 1911.01547, 2019). The arcprize.org page for ARC-AGI-1 was not fetched in this run, so the grid-puzzle format is stated from general knowledge, not from a source read here. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the maintainer; the attribution appears to reflect that OpenAI's model results are reported on it.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-1 is a set of colored grid puzzles where the model sees a few input and output examples and must work out the rule for a new input. Its creator designed it to measure how efficiently a system learns a new skill from very few examples, rather than how much it has memorised. It was the first of the ARC-AGI series and was not beaten by AI systems for about five years after it appeared.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: ARC Prize; co-founded by François Chollet and Mike Knoop. Launched 2025-03-24 per the ARC Prize announcements summarised in search results. Printed labels say Google and OpenAI, but these labs are only the companies whose models are scored on it; ARC Prize maintains it. A later figure of 68.8 percent for Claude Opus 4.6 came from an unverified wiki and is not used.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-2 is a harder successor to ARC-AGI-1 that keeps the same kind of puzzle but is built so that brute-force compute does not solve it. It measures how well a system learns new rules from a few examples. At launch in March 2025, human testers averaged about 60 percent, while leading AI reasoning models scored about 1 percent.

about.notes: Launched 2026-03-25 per the ARC Prize launch post. The post reports humans at 100 percent and frontier AI at 0.51 percent at launch; a DataCamp write-up gives 0.26 percent, so that figure is not used here. Printed label says OpenAI, which is not the maintainer.
about.what_it_tests: ARC-AGI-3 is the first fully interactive benchmark in the ARC series, made of hundreds of turn-based environments and thousands of game-style levels designed by human game designers. The agent gets no instructions, rules or goals, so it must explore, work out how each environment behaves and what winning means, and carry that understanding into harder levels. It measures whether a system can learn and adapt to unfamiliar situations rather than follow instructions.

about.notes: The methodology page lists v1.0 in May to June 2026 and says v1.5 is current, replacing Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Terminal-Bench 4.0 and upgrading DeepSWE to v1.1. The family label 'v1.4' is therefore superseded. The 'printed by OpenAI' label is not confirmed; comparison pages pair the index with Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build.
about.what_it_tests: The Coding Agent Index is a single score from Artificial Analysis for coding agents, meaning full tool setups such as Claude Code or Codex rather than models alone. It is an equal-weight average of benchmark components, which at v1.4 were DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas-QnA, a test of answering questions by tracing a code repository. Each component is scored as pass@1 averaged over three attempts per task, and reward-hacked or time-limited attempts score zero.

about.notes: The job label says v4.1.1, but the methodology page fetched on 2026-10-14 names v4.3.2 as current and its version history was not readable. The year is from a secondary source saying v4 launched in January 2026. Both OpenAI and xAI print this index, so the label is a third-party index that the labs cite, not their own test.
about.what_it_tests: The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index combines several test suites of primarily text-based, English-language tasks into one score for a language model. Its methodology page groups the evaluations into agents, coding, general knowledge and scientific reasoning, with a weight for each. The score is a weighted average, and agent tests are converted from Elo ratings to a 0 to 1 contribution.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (paper authors Daniel Shepard and Robin Salimans); Artificial Analysis runs the AutomationBench-AA leaderboard in partnership with Zapier. The benchmark has several versions and scores differ by version and source: the Zapier public leaderboard, the Artificial Analysis guardrail-based AutomationBench-AA (657 private tasks, announced July 6, 2026), and BenchLM private-set figures are not comparable. The arXiv abstract says even the best frontier models scored below 10 percent at release. The printed-by labels (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba) were not checked against model cards.
about.what_it_tests: AutomationBench tests whether AI agents can carry out business workflows that span several software applications, such as a CRM, an inbox, a calendar and a messaging tool, through their REST APIs. The agent has to find the right endpoints on its own, follow layered business rules, and ignore misleading records along the way. Grading is programmatic: the final state of the simulated systems is checked against success criteria, so a run is judged on the end result.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

about.maintainer: Authors of the May 2026 arXiv paper
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (listed as Haozhe Zhang, Kaichen Liu and Hanjie Chen by an aggregator); a host organisation is not confirmed, and no OpenAI link was found. The job label says OpenAI prints this benchmark, but I found only the academic arXiv paper and no OpenAI publication or card that uses it, so the printed attribution is unconfirmed. Independent leaderboard numbers were not found.
about.what_it_tests: BenchCAD is a benchmark of 17,900 industrial CAD programs written in CadQuery, each checked by running it, across 106 part families such as gears, springs and drill bits. Models answer questions about drawings and code, turn an image into code, and edit code according to an instruction. The authors report that current models often capture the rough outer shape of a part but struggle to build faithful parametric programs.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (San Francisco company); xAI prints the scores in its Grok 4.6 reporting. Refusal paper is arXiv 2607.05462; Surveillance is arXiv 2607.19262; Function is a preprint listed on Sciety (doi 10.64898/2026.09.03.749010). The xAI Grok 4.6 post (x.ai/news/biosafety-at-the-frontier) names BioSecBench-Refusal and BioSecBench-Surveillance and gives scores for Grok 4.6; the post is the source for the xAI attribution. Scores are not repeated here because they are vendor-reported.
about.what_it_tests: BioSecBench is a family of three checkable tests from LatchBio for AI agents doing biology work with a biosecurity angle. The Refusal part pairs routine research tasks with tasks that look like research but hide a hazard, and measures how often an agent refuses. The Surveillance part checks whether an agent can run pathogen genomic surveillance analyses correctly, and the Function part checks whether an agent can infer biological function from experimental data, scored against ground truth.

about.maintainer: SecureBio publishes the Virology Capabilities Test this label appears to derive from
about.notes: Maintainer detail: attribution of this specific subset to SecureBio is not confirmed. The aggregator says the public VCT paper does not expose this exact subset and treats the figure as display only. The Grok 4.6 model card itself was not accessible, so the subset and its score are unverified. See the virology-capabilities-test entry for the public benchmark.
about.what_it_tests: A biosecurity subset of the Virology Capabilities Test, scored by accuracy. The underlying test is a set of multiple-choice questions on troubleshooting complex virology lab protocols, written with expert virologists. The exact subset and how it was selected are not published.

about.notes: The closest match found is BioSecBench-Refusal (LatchBio, arXiv 2607.05462), which the name may be a mislabel of; a separate RefusalBench paper (arXiv 2605.21545) is a different benchmark. One aggregator (BenchLM) lists a BioUseBench refusal figure for Grok 4.6 and calls it self-reported; that figure is unverified.
about.what_it_tests: By its name, a test of how often a model refuses dual-use biology requests, meaning requests that could help research or cause harm. No published description of its design or scoring exists under this name.

about.notes: Announced March 2025 (paper Mitchener et al., arXiv 2503.00096). The original paper reported 17% open-answer accuracy for Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The catalog label zero-shot MCQ accuracy refers to the multiple-choice grading mode. Later subset results (BixBench-Verified-50) are self-reported by vendors and are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: BixBench tests whether AI agents can do realistic bioinformatics analysis. The benchmark has 53 analysis scenarios built from published research notebooks, with 296 questions in total. An agent receives the data and must run the analysis and answer, and answers are graded either open-ended or as multiple choice.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: Jason Wei, Zhiqing Sun and about eight other OpenAI co-authors. Released April 2025; the paper is arXiv 2504.12516. Official data is distributed through OpenAI's simple-evals repository in encrypted form. Printed labels Google and xAI are not confirmed by any source found; they are presumably companies that report results on it.
about.what_it_tests: BrowseComp tests whether an AI agent with web browsing can find hard-to-locate facts that are spread across many sources and tied together. It has 1,266 questions with short answers that are easy to check against a reference. Models without browsing scored near zero when it was released, and a browsing agent solved about half of the questions.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (the benchmark sits in the huggingface GitHub organisation); xAI prints the scores. Leaderboard figures in aggregators conflict across snapshots, so no score is given here; the official Hugging Face leaderboard is the place to check. The reward label printed by xAI is not explained by the repository.
about.what_it_tests: CADGenBench judges whether AI systems can produce usable 3D mechanical parts. It has two tasks: build a valid, geometrically correct 3D model from an engineering drawing, and edit an existing STEP file to apply a requested change. Each sample gets one STEP or BREP file, and scoring runs on a leaderboard against ground truth that stays private.

about.notes: Printed label says xAI. The xAI Grok 4.7 launch page (https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7) does not mention CathedralBench, and no other source was found. The aggregator's developer field and its score figures could not be verified, so no score is given here. Maintainer left null because the printed xAI attribution is unconfirmed.
about.what_it_tests: CathedralBench is described by one third-party tracker as a multi-step cyber challenge run without safeguards, where a result is reported only on the hardest tasks. It is meant to show what the underlying model can do when it is not restricted. This description is secondhand and comes from an aggregator page, not from a primary source.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: authors Suhaas Garre, Chris Mutty, Sushant Mehta and Edwin Chen; the Hugging Face dataset is under the surgeai namespace. arXiv 2608.10677, submitted August 11, 2026. The paper reports mean pass@1 over 30 model configurations with 20 trials per task. The arXiv page does not describe how an individual answer is judged beyond the expert ranges. The 'with tools' variant is a catalog label; aggregators report it, and the paper's tool setup was not confirmed here.
about.what_it_tests: Chartography tests whether AI models can read and reason about professional charts, such as Kaplan-Meier survival curves, candlestick charts, Sankey diagrams and Bode plots, which standard chart tests rarely include. It has 100 tasks written by professionals in fields such as medicine, engineering, finance and manufacturing. Numeric answers are checked against ranges set by the expert author, and scores are averaged over repeated runs.

No independent evaluation or paper was found. The year is inferred from the Qwen3.8 release, not from a stated introduction date. about.what_it_tests: CoWorkBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark for long-horizon professional work across computer science, finance, law, medicine and other productivity domains. Its grading method is not published.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

The page's changelog starts with version 3.0 on March 11, 2026, and version 4.0 is dated September 10, 2026. Scores are only comparable within one version. Cursor's page and its mirrors show different leaders for different snapshots. The 'printed by Anthropic, xAI' labels were not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: CursorBench is Cursor's own coding-agent benchmark, built from ambiguous, multi-file tasks taken from real Cursor sessions. Version 4.0 adds long-horizon work such as editing, refactoring, investigation and managing jobs. Each agent gets a percentage score, and the page also reports cost per task and tokens used.

about.maintainer: Yuxuan Zhu, Daniel Kang and co-authors
about.notes: Maintainer detail: paper published at ICML 2025. Printed label says xAI. The xAI Grok 4.7 launch page does not mention CVE-Bench, so the xAI attribution is unconfirmed. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists CVE-Bench as a cyber evaluation that was retired after it became saturated, so the name appears in OpenAI's card too.
about.what_it_tests: CVE-Bench measures whether AI agents can succeed against 40 real, serious web application vulnerabilities taken from the US national vulnerability database. The targets are content management systems and AI applications, and each attempt is checked automatically inside a sandbox. The paper's headline finding is that the best agent framework succeeded on up to 13 percent of the vulnerabilities.

about.notes: Printed label says Google, and no Google source was found; the attribution is unconfirmed. The cwe-bench.com page names no maintainer and no paper, and the year of introduction is not stated. A separate CWE-bench launched by Collinear AI on 2026-09-02 (100 tasks, 54 weakness types) was found; it is not confirmed to be the same benchmark as cwe-bench.com, so it is not used here. Aggregators name a Google model as top scorer, which is a leaderboard fact and not a maintainer fact.
about.what_it_tests: The leaderboard page describes CWE-Bench as a benchmark that evaluates autonomous agents on finding and patching real-world software vulnerabilities. The page does not describe the task format or the scoring method in more detail. It only links to an implementation page and a dataset at the same site.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

about.maintainer: UC Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Berkeley RDI); authors Zhun Wang, Tianneng Shi, Jingxuan He, Matthew Cai, Jialin Zhang and Dawn Song. The paper (arXiv 2506.02548, first posted June 2025) was published at ICLR 2026. Printed label says xAI, and the xAI Grok 4.7 launch page does not mention CyberGym, so that attribution is unconfirmed. The RDI page links a live observatory at https://rdi.berkeley.edu/frontier-ai-impact-on-cybersecurity/benchmarks.html for leaderboard results.
about.what_it_tests: CyberGym tests whether AI agents can reproduce real vulnerabilities in open-source software. The agent gets a vulnerable codebase and a written description, and must write a test input that makes the bug crash the code before the fix but not after it. The benchmark has 1,507 vulnerabilities across 188 open-source projects, and each attempt is checked automatically with sanitizers.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: authors Wenqi Huang, Charley Lee, Leonard Tng and Serena Ge. The fetched launch post (May 26, 2026) describes v1.0. The page links to v1.1 as the latest version, which this description does not cover. The 'printed by Google, OpenAI, xAI, Alibaba' labels were not verified in model cards.
about.what_it_tests: DeepSWE tests whether coding agents can make original, long-horizon software engineering changes in real open-source repositories. It has 113 tasks across 91 repositories in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust, all written from scratch so that solutions are not copied from existing commits. Hand-written verifiers check behavior through public interfaces, and each verifier runs three times to catch flakiness.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: (per an aggregator); not confirmed from the project itself. Do not confuse with EEE-Bench (CVPR 2025), a separate multimodal electrical and electronics benchmark. One aggregator page describes EEBench as a physics-simulation framework, which conflicts with the other sources and was not used. The eebench.org site was not opened.
about.what_it_tests: EEBench is an agent benchmark about electrical engineering, with scores shown on a public leaderboard. Its tasks and the meaning of the printed reward are not published in detail.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: Carnegie Mellon University per secondary coverage; affiliations not shown on the arXiv page. Printed label says OpenAI, which does not match the public benchmark: its authors are academic, and the arXiv paper was posted 2026-05-13. The GPT-6 Astra system card (https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra/) lists ExploitBench and a separate 'ExploitBench - Internal Port (June-August 2026)' that uses only vulnerabilities disclosed after the model's knowledge cutoff. The internal port is OpenAI-only; the public benchmark is not.
about.what_it_tests: ExploitBench measures how far an AI agent gets along a ladder of 16 checkable capability steps when it works on known, already-patched bugs in the V8 JavaScript engine used by Chromium. The steps run from triggering the bug up to full control of the target, and each step is confirmed by an automatic verifier with no AI judge. The public set has 41 bugs, all reported in 2024 or later.

about.maintainer: Academic author team led by UC Berkeley researchers
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (Zhun Wang, Dawn Song and co-authors) with contributors from several universities; secondary coverage also lists staff from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google among the co-authors. Printed label says OpenAI. The arXiv page does not show affiliations, and the lead team is academic, so OpenAI is not the maintainer. The GPT-6 Astra system card lists ExploitGym as an OpenAI cyber evaluation and a separate honeypot test built on it, so OpenAI does use it. The preprint date is 2026-05-11 on arXiv; a secondary write-up cites 2026-07-22 for results, which is not used here.
about.what_it_tests: ExploitGym measures whether AI agents can take a program input that already triggers a software vulnerability and turn it step by step into a working attack. The benchmark has 898 instances in three areas: ordinary user programs, a JavaScript engine, and the Linux kernel. Protections are varied from task to task to see how they change agent success, and every task runs in a reproducible container.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (internal variant, per the printed label); the public ExploitGym benchmark is described in an arXiv paper whose author list I did not confirm. The arXiv paper is the public base benchmark, not confirmed to be the same as the internal honeypot variant. Secondary coverage in July 2026 linked an OpenAI evaluation to an incident involving Hugging Face; those are secondary accounts and are not used in this description.
about.what_it_tests: The public ExploitGym benchmark asks whether AI agents can turn a vulnerability-triggering input into a working exploit. It has 898 instances drawn from userspace programs, Google's V8 JavaScript engine and the Linux kernel, and each instance comes with a vulnerable codebase and an execution environment. What the honeypot variant changes is not published; the score is read as lower is better.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: with Stanford researchers, per the arXiv paper. The arXiv paper 2508.00828 dates the original benchmark to August 2025. The Vals page (dated October 12, 2026) says v2 builds on v1.1 and gives its scoring modes. Leaderboard figures differ by snapshot, and the 'printed by Google' label was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: Finance Agent tests AI agents on research tasks that a financial analyst would do, such as answering questions from recent SEC filings. The original version had 537 expert-written questions in nine task categories, and the agent is given search and EDGAR database access. Version 2 contains 927 expert-reviewed questions, and results are reported as partial credit or as all-pass, where a fully correct answer is required.

about.maintainer: Cognition, built with maintainers of 36 open-source repositories
about.notes: Cognition announced the benchmark in June 2026 and released version 1.1 in July 2026. Cognition's own announcement page was not located, so the description rests on the Artificial Analysis article (published October 12, 2026). Epoch AI describes Main and Extended subsets, while the Artificial Analysis article describes only Main. The 'printed by Anthropic, OpenAI' labels were not confirmed.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierCode tests whether an AI coding agent's change to a real open-source project is good enough for that project's maintainers to merge, not just code that passes tests. It has 150 tasks drawn from 36 repositories, and Artificial Analysis runs the 100-task Main set with three attempts per task. Each attempt must pass deterministic tests and file-scope limits, and an LLM judge checks it against maintainer criteria, where failing any blocking check scores zero.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: OpenAI commissioned part of the problems and supported creation, per Epoch's page. The earliest dated version on Epoch's page is FrontierMath_10-22-24. Tier 4 development finished June 2025 per the page. The June 12, 2026 date for v2 comes from the Tier 4 v2 benchmark page. Scores are not listed; the 'saturated' claim comes from one news aggregator and is not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierMath is a set of research-level mathematics problems written by professional mathematicians across most branches of modern maths. Tier 4 is its hardest part, with 43 problems in version 2 (released June 12, 2026). Answers are checked automatically: the model must submit a short Python function that returns the final answer within 30 seconds, and each problem scores 1 or 0.

about.notes: The GitHub repository was not fetched, and the original launch date is unclear: sources give June 2026 and July 2026 (version 1, 17 tasks). Version 2 was released in September 2026. Model results come from Proximal's own harness, which the team notes is evaluation-aware, and Proximal reports cheating episodes that were zeroed. Independent reproduction is not yet available.
about.what_it_tests: FrontierSWE tests coding agents on very long engineering and research jobs: reimplementing complex systems, speeding up existing code without breaking its correctness, and designing and training machine learning models on held-out data. Version 2 has 34 tasks, each with up to a 20-hour budget per trial. Results are averaged over five trials per task (mean at 5).

about.maintainer: Artificial Analysis, which runs its own version of OpenAI's GDPval dataset
about.notes: The canonical URL is inferred from the Artificial Analysis evaluation URL pattern and the search result; the methodology page returned 404 when fetched. The launch year was not stated in the sources read. BenchLM reports a different normalized-percentage metric, and the Elo leaderboard figures were not verified on the primary site.
about.what_it_tests: GDPval-AA is Artificial Analysis's version of OpenAI's GDPval, a set of realistic work tasks drawn from 44 occupations in nine major industries. Models get shell access and web browsing in an agent loop and produce a work product, and the outputs are compared in blind pairwise judgments that are turned into Elo ratings. The v2 revision re-anchors the scale so that human-expert deliverables sit near 1000 points.

about.notes: The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 when read, so the facts come from secondary coverage that agrees on a June 30, 2026 release and the 129-problem count. One outlet describes it as 10 genomics case studies, which conflicts with the count. Ten questions were said to be open-sourced on Hugging Face; not verified.
about.what_it_tests: GeneBench-Pro tests AI agents on computational biology work where no single method is obviously right. It contains 129 problems across 10 domains and 21 subdomains, including statistical genetics, cancer genomics, clinical diagnostics and pharmacogenomics. OpenAI describes it as measuring judgement about analysis choices rather than factual recall, and grading is deterministic.

about.maintainer: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, Jackson Petty, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Julien Dirani, Julian Michael and Samuel R. Bowman
about.notes: Maintainer detail: GPQA authors. The arXiv abstract page does not mention a Diamond subset, so its definition was not confirmed here. The 448-question count and the expert and non-expert accuracies come from the page. Publisher-printed results from several labs are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: GPQA is a set of 448 multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by experts with or working toward PhDs in those fields. Domain experts reached about 65% accuracy, while skilled non-experts with web access reached about 34%, which is why the questions are described as hard to answer by search alone. The Diamond subset is a smaller, harder selection of these questions.

about.notes: Epoch AI's review credits OpenAI as creator and rates the benchmark Verified (1,150 tasks, independently reproduced). The original release date and an OpenAI primary page were not found, so url and year are null. The 128k and 256k-1M ranges are from catalog labels; no scores are given.
about.what_it_tests: GraphWalks tests whether a model can follow connections through a very long list of directed edges that define a graph. Given the edges, the model must either list every node with an edge pointing into a given node, or list the nodes reachable at a chosen depth from a starting node, in one answer with no tools. Answers are scored with F1, which combines how many correct nodes were found with how many listed nodes were correct.

about.notes: The xAI Grok 4.7 model card could not be retrieved: the data.x.ai URL that was guessed returned 404 and no search result gave the card's address. The launch page is the only primary source found. An aggregator (BenchLM) describes a HackerBench v0.2 measuring benign refusal, which the launch page does not mention; that version is not confirmed and is not described here. The year of introduction is not stated.
about.what_it_tests: The xAI Grok 4.7 launch page calls HackerBench v0.3 its own benchmark for risky and malicious cyber tasks. The reported result is the share of risky dual-use prompts that the model let through, and the page says Grok 4.7 let through 3.3 percent while showing the highest safety of the models compared. The page does not explain how prompts are built or how each answer is judged.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: (open-source repository harveyai/harvey-labs); Artificial Analysis and Mercor run separate third-party evaluations. Announced May 6, 2026, and launched without a leaderboard. Task counts differ across sources: the page cites 1,200 and 1,250 tasks, Mercor lists 1,749. Third-party rankings exist (Mercor, and an Artificial Analysis private set of 120 tasks). The 'Google, xAI printed' labels were not confirmed in a model card.
about.what_it_tests: Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark tests AI agents on long, multi-step legal work. Each task gives the agent a short instruction and a client matter with case files, and asks for a work product that a reviewing lawyer would check, across more than 1,200 tasks in 24 legal practice areas. Expert-written rubrics grade each deliverable, and a task counts as passed only when every criterion passes.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: developed with 262 physicians from 60 countries. Paper: arXiv 2505.08775 (May 2025). Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. The paper uses GPT-4.1 as the automatic rubric scorer. The GPT-6 Astra system card reports HealthBench as a length-adjusted score, where higher is better.
about.what_it_tests: HealthBench tests how well an AI model answers health conversations, such as those with patients or clinicians, judged against detailed rubrics written by physicians. It has 5,000 multi-turn conversations and 48,562 rubric criteria, each with a weight that reflects how much a physician would value it. An automatic grader scores each reply against the rubric, and the benchmark includes subsets named Consensus and Hard.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: rubrics written and adjudicated by three or more physicians across three phases. Paper: arXiv 2604.27470. OpenAI built the benchmark and also reports results for its own clinician product, so it is not an independent test; the caveat appears in secondary coverage. xAI's Grok 4.7 launch page does report HealthBench Professional (56.7 percent for Grok 4.7). The 'length-adjusted' label is confirmed for HealthBench, not for HealthBench Professional, where the GPT-6 Astra card says only 'higher is better'. Aggregator leaderboards disagree on the top model, so no score is given.
about.what_it_tests: HealthBench Professional tests AI models on real conversations that clinicians had with an AI assistant, in three areas: care consultation, writing and documentation, and medical research. Each example is scored against rubrics written and checked by at least three physicians. It is meant to be hard, and about a third of the examples were chosen because physicians deliberately tried to find failures.

about.maintainer: Center for AI Safety (CAIS) and Scale AI
about.notes: The arXiv preprint is 2501.14249 (January 2025); a later version was published in Nature in February 2026 under the title 'A benchmark of expert-level academic questions to assess AI capabilities'. Question counts differ by source (2,500 in the paper; about 3,000 in press coverage), so the paper's figure is used. The family label 'HLE with tools' is a configuration of the same benchmark and is not described separately.
about.what_it_tests: Humanity's Last Exam is a test of about 2,500 expert-level questions across dozens of subjects, including mathematics, the humanities and the natural sciences. The items are multiple-choice or short-answer, so answers can be graded automatically. It was built because leading models had passed more than 90 percent of older tests, and at launch the most capable models scored below 10 percent.

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington
about.notes: Maintainer detail: Valentina Pyatkin and co-authors. Title of the paper: 'Generalizing Verifiable Instruction Following', published at NeurIPS 2025 (Datasets and Benchmarks track). Printed label says Alibaba, which no source confirms. A third-party summary's 17 to 26 point gain from training is not verified against the paper and is not used.
about.what_it_tests: IFBench tests whether a language model follows written instructions that carry checkable constraints, such as counting, formatting, and word or character rules. It uses 58 new constraints that the models were not trained on, so it measures generalisation rather than memorised rules. Each reply is checked automatically by a rule-based function, and the paper reports that leading models of the time scored below 50 percent on the new constraints.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (internal, per the printed label); not confirmed. Secondary write-ups (an external investigation by METR and Redwood Research, cited second-hand) discuss unsolvable ExploitGym tasks, but they do not describe a benchmark named Impossible ExploitGym. The datalearner page for the name redirects to another site and gave no content.
about.what_it_tests: From the name alone, this is a variant of ExploitGym, the public exploit benchmark, that likely includes tasks which cannot be solved as designed. I found no source that describes this variant, so what it measures and how it is scored are unconfirmed.

about.maintainer: Paper authors Yuetai Li, Xiang Yue, Radha Poovendran and others
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (affiliations not shown on the abstract page); Alibaba attribution not confirmed. The paper was submitted May 25, 2026. Its author list shows no Alibaba affiliation on the page read, so the aggregator's Alibaba label is unconfirmed; this may be a different benchmark from any Alibaba-printed one. The paper reports the best of 36 models at 45.9 percent (Claude Opus 4.7 under Claude Code). The BenchLM figure of 33.4 for Qwen3.8-27B was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: JobBench tests AI agents on professional work that experts say they would want to hand off to an agent, rather than on tasks chosen for their economic value. It has 130 tasks across 35 occupations, and each task is a workspace of mixed and sometimes conflicting reference files that the agent must sort through. Outputs are graded against chains of rubrics that average about 35.6 binary criteria per task.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.
Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: first author Jon M. Laurent, with Samuel Rodriques and co-authors. arXiv 2407.10362, first submitted July 14, 2024. The successor LABBench2 (arXiv 2604.09554, FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, first submitted February 4, 2026) is a separate entry under the same family. The public release holds about 80% of the data, per the GitHub repository.
about.what_it_tests: LAB-Bench is a set of more than 2,400 multiple-choice questions that test practical biology research skills for language models and AI agents. The categories include recalling and reasoning over scientific literature, interpreting figures, using biology databases, and working with DNA and protein sequences. Models are scored on the share of questions they answer correctly and are compared with human expert biology researchers.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

The benchmarks.bio page describes 13 component benchmarks and a weighted average; aggregators describe 11 and an equal-weight mean, so these conflict. The v1.0 release date was not confirmed. Scores are not listed because aggregator figures disagree on the model set. The harness used to run the agent is reported separately and affects scores.
about.what_it_tests: LatchBio Capabilities is a composite score for how well AI agents analyse real biological data. Each component benchmark starts from a snapshot of real experimental data taken just before a key analysis step, and the agent must work out the biological result. A deterministic grader checks each answer, and the overall score is a weighted average of the pass rates.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: with 173 scientists and Tacit Labs (a drug-development feedback startup) writing the tasks. The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 when read. The June 17, 2026 date and the task counts come from secondary coverage (AI Weekly, Let's Data Science, Gigazine), which agree. A reader comment says the questions are not public; not confirmed. Scores are omitted.
about.what_it_tests: LifeSciBench tests AI on the judgement work life-science researchers do, such as interpreting incomplete evidence, troubleshooting experiments and deciding what to do next. It has 750 expert-written tasks across seven workflows and seven biological domains. Each task includes supporting material and a grading rubric, and the answer is checked against that rubric (19,020 criteria in total).

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (with Zhipu AI); LongBench v2 authors include Yushi Bai and Shangqing Tu. Family dates from the original LongBench (arXiv 2308.14508, 2023, ACL 2024). LongBench v2 (arXiv 2412.15204) is from December 2024. The human baseline is 53.7% per the paper. Model scores are not repeated.
about.what_it_tests: LongBench v2 tests whether language models can reason over very long inputs, with contexts from about 8,000 to 2 million words. It has 503 multiple-choice questions in six categories: single-document and multi-document question answering, long in-context learning, long dialogue history, code repository understanding and long structured data. Human experts scored about 54% under a 15-minute limit, which is the reference point for model scores.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: first author Weihan Wang. The paper is arXiv 2406.08035 (June 2024), published at ICCV 2025. The video and question counts come from a third-party alphaXiv summary and were not checked against the paper's full text. Model scores are not given.
about.what_it_tests: LVBench tests whether vision-language models can understand very long videos, where the key facts can be spread across more than an hour of footage. It contains about 100 videos averaging over an hour, with roughly 1,500 question-answer pairs across six temporal comprehension tasks. Models are scored on accuracy against human performance.

about.maintainer: Center for AI Safety and Scale AI wrote the base MASK benchmark
about.notes: Maintainer detail: the rectified variant appears to come from xAI's own implementation (unconfirmed. I could not find what the rectification changes, so the MASK-Rectified scores (printed as a dishonesty rate, lower is better) are unverified. The only source for the variant is a third-party aggregator; the base MASK leaderboard is at labs.scale.com/leaderboard/mask.
about.what_it_tests: The base MASK benchmark tests whether a model lies under pressure, which is a different question from whether it knows the right answer. It first checks what a model believes, then pressures it to contradict that belief, and scores honesty separately from accuracy. The authors report that larger models become more accurate on the benchmark but do not become more honest.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.
Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer page was not checked.

Could not confirm the benchmark in an OpenAI system card. Aggregators disagree on the top model and score (one lists GPT-5.6 Sol at 48.3%, another GPT-6 Astra at 49.7%), and one aggregator attributes it to a GPT-Rosalind-5.5 card. BenchLM's medicinal chemistry table is a different, Anthropic-reported benchmark. The release date is unknown.
about.what_it_tests: MedChemBench is an internal OpenAI evaluation of medicinal chemistry reasoning, meant to test whether a model can support drug-discovery chemistry work: reading chemical structures, predicting properties such as potency or toxicity, comparing candidate molecules and planning synthesis routes. The task set and the scoring are not published.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (catalog hint, not confirmed for the Lite subset). The MLS-Bench paper lists 28 authors including Chi Jin, Dawn Song and Max Simchowitz. The arXiv abstract page confirms MLS-Bench (first version May 9, 2026; v3 July 6, 2026) but does not mention Lite. The 30-task Lite subset comes only from aggregators (LLM Reference, BenchLM, benchmarklist). LLM Reference describes its scores as Moonshot-reported from Kimi launch materials, so the Lite maintainer is unconfirmed.
about.what_it_tests: MLS-Bench asks whether an AI system can invent machine learning methods that generalise and scale, rather than only tuning existing ones. Each of its 140 tasks asks an agent to improve one component of an ML system and then show the gain holds across controlled settings. MLS-Bench-Lite is a 30-task subset that covers all 12 domains of the full benchmark at a fraction of the compute.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.
Maintainer page was not checked.

about.maintainer: Kiran Vodrahalli and co-authors of the Michelangelo paper
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (listed by one wiki as Google DeepMind); the public MRCR dataset is attributed to OpenAI. The Michelangelo paper (arXiv 2409.12640, September 2024) defines MRCR as one of three tasks. The OpenAI release of the dataset was not confirmed on a primary source. The 8-needle and 256K-1M details come from benchmark listings, not the paper. Scores are omitted because listings disagree.
about.what_it_tests: MRCR (Multi-Round Coreference Resolution) tests whether a model can find one specific earlier item in a very long chat. The conversation contains many similar requests, such as poems or essays on overlapping topics, and the model must reproduce the output that matches the one the user asked for. The 8-needle variant hides eight such matching items, and results are reported at long context lengths such as 256K, 512K and 1M tokens.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: (first author Jingzhe Ding; 49 authors on arXiv; affiliations not shown on the abstract page); Alibaba attribution not confirmed. arXiv 2512.12730 was posted in December 2025 and accepted to ICML 2026 (PMLR 306). The abstract reports that even the strongest agents average below 40 percent test pass rate. The Alibaba label was not supported by the affiliations read.
about.what_it_tests: NL2Repo-Bench tests whether a coding agent can build a whole software project from a single natural-language requirements document. The agent starts with an empty workspace and must produce an installable Python library, across 104 tasks in nine library categories graded as easy, medium and hard. Scoring is execution-based, measuring the average share of each project's tests that pass.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.
Maintainer page was not checked.

about.maintainer: Paper authors from Humanlaya, BIGAI, xbench and M-A-P
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (per the arXiv affiliations); the aggregator's Alibaba label is not supported by the paper. The first version was submitted March 9, 2026 and the current version was revised October 8, 2026. Project code is at github.com/humanlaya/OneMillion-Bench. The expert-score leaderboard seen on a third-party site (dated 2026-08-03) was not verified and its model names were not captured.
about.what_it_tests: $OneMillion-Bench tests language agents on 400 expert-curated professional tasks in law, finance, industry, healthcare and natural science. The tasks ask agents to find authoritative sources, resolve conflicting evidence, apply domain rules and make constrained decisions, and each task carries a dollar value based on the time a senior professional would need. Responses are scored with an expert rubric covering factual accuracy, logical coherence, practical feasibility and professional compliance.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: publisher-internal evaluation, described in the GPT-6 Astra system card. The exact name 'OpenAI Factuality on Flagged Conversations' does not appear in the card; the closest entry is the one titled 'Performance in Cases Flagged by Users', so the mapping is a judgment. The card is dated 2026-09-03. A search for the exact name returned only generic OpenAI factuality method text from the GPT-5 system card, which is not the same evaluation.
about.what_it_tests: An entry in the GPT-6 Astra system card titled 'Performance in Cases Flagged by Users', which covers factual errors, including whether the model reproduces errors that users have flagged. The card reports these as error rates where lower is better. The test set itself is internal.

about.notes: The GPT-6 Astra system card was not accessible; a secondary report says it is posted on OpenAI's Deployment Safety Hub. This description rests on the printed name only.
about.what_it_tests: By its name, this internal OpenAI evaluation checks whether a model tells the user when its search tool is broken or returns errors, rather than presenting results as if they were fine. The score is a failure-to-disclose measure as printed. I did not find OpenAI's own description of it.

about.notes: The GPT-6 Astra system card was not accessible, so this description is based on the name and the printed direction of the score only.
about.what_it_tests: By its name, this internal OpenAI benchmark measures how often a model tries to circumvent restrictions or safeguards placed on its work. Lower is better, as printed. I did not find OpenAI's own description of the test items or the scoring.

about.notes: Unverified. The GPT-6 Astra system card was not accessible; a secondary source says Astra supports computer use, which is consistent with this label but does not describe the evaluation.
about.what_it_tests: An internal OpenAI benchmark that tests the safety of computer-use agents, which are models that operate a computer on a user's behalf. OpenAI has not published the tasks or the scoring.

about.notes: Searched for an OpenAI system card reporting this benchmark and found none. Two aggregators (AI Release Tracker and DataLearnerAI) list a single entry attached to a 2026 model release, but that is a secondary claim that could not be checked against OpenAI's documents. The OpenAI system card or model card that would hold the description was not located.
about.what_it_tests: A set of data-science tasks used inside OpenAI, where a model takes a dataset and a question through cleaning, analysis and a defensible answer. The task set and the scoring are not published.

about.notes: The description and score come only from a third-party aggregator. Searches for an OpenAI system card or model card that describes this internal evaluation returned nothing usable, so the description is unconfirmed and the score may not be from OpenAI's own release material.
about.what_it_tests: OpenAI's own test of moving a database from one schema or system to another without breaking the things that depend on it. The task set and the scoring are internal to OpenAI.

about.notes: Name-only description. The GPT-6 Astra system card was not accessible.
about.what_it_tests: By its name alone, this is an internal OpenAI evaluation of design tasks, which may cover producing or editing visual designs. I did not find OpenAI's description of the tasks, inputs or scoring.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: publisher-internal; no system card found that defines it. Not found: no system card in this run names an 'OpenAI Internal Hallucination' benchmark. The GPT-6 Astra card's entry 'Performance in Cases Flagged by Users' may be the same measure, but this is not confirmed. A different internal test, PersonQA ('OpenAI's internal PersonQA benchmark' in the o3 system card, where lower is better), exists and is not the same name; it is not described here.
about.what_it_tests: An OpenAI internal hallucination benchmark where lower scores are better: it measures how often a model states false facts. OpenAI has not published a description under this name.

about.maintainer: Dongmin Kim, Brian Liu, Jose J. Valero-Mas and Dasaem Jeong
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (authors of OSSQ-OMR), built on the OpenScore String Quartet corpus from the OpenScore project. arXiv 2608.10978, submitted August 11, 2026, accepted to ISMIR 2026. The page does not mention OpenAI, so the catalog's OpenAI attribution is not supported. The page reports OMR-NED values but does not define the metric; the 'higher is better' reading of one minus OMR-NED is inferred from the name.
about.what_it_tests: This benchmark tests optical music recognition: whether software can read a page of sheet music and write it out in a machine-readable notation. It uses string quartet scores, where several instrument parts play together, with 116 scores from the OpenScore corpus paired with scanned editions from IMSLP. The score is one minus OMR-NED, a normalised edit-distance measure of how far the transcription is from the correct one, so higher is better.

about.maintainer: XLANG Lab, University of Hong Kong
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (OSWorld 2.0 collaborators include Columbia, UC Santa Barbara, UC San Diego, Mila, Snorkel AI, Alibaba Qwen and Simular). The original 2024 OSWorld paper lists Tianbao Xie, Tao Yu and others. The original OSWorld paper (arXiv 2404.07972, April 2024) has 369 tasks and execution-based scoring. The OSWorld 2.0 release date was not stated on its page and is not confirmed. OSWorld 2.1 partial was not researched. Leaderboard figures conflict across sources, so none are given.
about.what_it_tests: OSWorld tests whether an AI agent can carry out open-ended tasks on a real computer desktop, on Ubuntu, Windows or macOS, by clicking and typing in real applications. OSWorld 2.0 has 108 long workflows across professional and everyday work, each taking a skilled human over an hour, with some changing mid-task and some requiring questions to the user. Success is binary completion within a 500-step limit, with a partial score for checkpoints reached.

about.notes: OpenAI released it April 2, 2025 and it was accepted to ICML 2025. Code is in the openai/preparedness GitHub repository. The launch-era score (21.0% for the best agent) is not repeated because later summaries give different ranges.
about.what_it_tests: PaperBench tests whether an AI agent can reproduce the results of recent machine learning research from scratch. The agent gets 20 papers from ICML 2024 and must write the code and run the experiments without the original code. Grading uses 8,316 rubric items written with the paper authors, and an automated AI judge scores each attempt.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: (Qwen Team), with Tsinghua University, University of Waterloo, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, University of Pittsburgh and University of Bologna (per the arXiv affiliations. Submitted January 23, 2026 (v2 January 28, 2026). Data is at github.com/skylenage/PLawbench. The evalscope documentation describes a 280-sample version split into subsets, which does not match the paper's 850 questions, so the counts depend on the release used. Not to be confused with the older LawBench (2023).
about.what_it_tests: PLawBench tests large language models on Chinese legal practice across 13 scenarios that follow a lawyer's workflow: public legal consultation, practical case analysis and drafting legal documents. It has 850 questions, and each has expert-written rubrics, about 12,500 items in total. An LLM evaluator aligned with human expert judgments scores each response against those rubrics.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: Ben Rank, Hardik Bhatnagar, Ameya Prabhu, Shira Eisenberg, Karina Nguyen, Matthias Bethge, Maksym Andriushchenko. arXiv version submitted March 9, 2026 (v2 March 10). Also listed at ICLR 2026 and ICML 2026. The catalog label v1.1 is not explained on the arXiv page. Agent scores differ between paper versions and the AISA Group post, so none are repeated here.
about.what_it_tests: PostTrainBench tests whether an AI agent can do post-training, the stage that turns a raw language model into a useful assistant. Each agent gets a small base model, one GPU and a 10-hour budget, and is free to pick data and methods to improve it on a target test. Scores compare the agent-trained model with the official instruction-tuned version, and the authors also track cheating such as training on test data.

about.notes: The arXiv paper (2511.11562) was submitted November 14, 2025 and the Scale page is dated November 13, 2025. The 600-task finance count and the 300-task Hard subset come from search snippets; the Scale page gives only the combined totals. The llm-stats figure of 0.583 for Qwen3.8 Max is a single self-reported entry and was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: PRBench-Finance is the finance half of PRBench, a set of open-ended professional reasoning tasks written by experts holding JDs, CFAs or six or more years of experience, drawn from real professional workflows. The full PRBench has 1,100 tasks, of which 600 are finance, and each answer is scored against expert-written rubric criteria. On the Hard finance subset, the best of 20 models scored only 0.39 at release.

about.notes: Same benchmark release as PRBench-Finance. The 500-task law count and the 250-task Hard subset come from search snippets; the paper and Scale page give the combined totals and the 0.37 top score. The jurisdiction wording was taken from the Scale page, which says tasks span 114 countries and 47 US jurisdictions. The llm-stats figure of 0.576 was not verified.
about.what_it_tests: PRBench-Legal is the law half of PRBench, a set of open-ended professional reasoning tasks written by experts holding JDs, CFAs or six or more years of experience, drawn from real professional workflows. The full PRBench has 1,100 tasks, of which 500 are law, and the full set spans 114 countries and 47 US jurisdictions. Each answer is scored against expert-written rubric criteria, and on the Hard legal subset the best of 20 models scored 0.37 at release.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

The LAB-Bench abstract page does not name ProtocolQA; the link to LAB-Bench comes from the GPT-5 system card and an aggregator. The original multiple-choice ProtocolQA set is cited as 135 questions by an aggregator. No xAI model card was found to confirm the Open-Ended table, so the xAI attribution is unverified.
about.what_it_tests: ProtocolQA tests whether a model can spot and fix mistakes in published lab protocols. In the open-ended form, each question describes a protocol with an error, gives the wet-lab result of following it, and asks how the procedure should be corrected. OpenAI's GPT-5 system card describes the open-ended form as short-answer versions of 108 multiple-choice questions from FutureHouse's ProtocolQA dataset.

about.notes: The task content is not described in the model card beyond the Qoder user-experience purpose. Aggregators disagree: LLM Stats lists one self-reported model, while BenchmarkList lists five models with a top score of 63.1 percent, dated 2026-08-03, which was not verified. No paper or methodology was found.
about.what_it_tests: QwenQoderBench is an in-house Qwen benchmark for coding agents, which the Qwen3.8 model card describes as an inhouse benchmark for evaluating user experience on Qoder. The card reports results from Qwen's own testing, and the 2.4T flagship card lists a score of 58.4. The benchmark measures coding-agent tasks, and BenchmarkList reports it as Avg@5.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: internal benchmark per the BenchLM aggregator. No Alibaba or Qwen primary source was found. Aggregators disagree on scores (LLM Stats lists one model at 1724; another listing shows a top score of 1770), and the results are vendor-reported, so no score is given. The Qwen launch post for the model that reported it is the place to check the method.
about.what_it_tests: According to an aggregator, QwenReactBench is Qwen's internal test of building and rendering bilingual React projects across seven categories. Generated projects are rendered, checked by a multimodal judge, and ranked with a Bradley-Terry Elo-style rating. These details come from a third-party page, not from an Alibaba publication.

about.notes: Maintainer detail: self-reported per one aggregator; no official Qwen source found. The name 'QwenSVGBench' did not match any Qwen publication in search. The only related listing uses the name 'QwenSVG', and the scores are self-reported and unverified. A separate independent SVG leaderboard (Design Arena SVG Elo) is a different benchmark and is not the same thing.
about.what_it_tests: A Qwen benchmark of generating SVG vector graphics, with vendor-reported Elo-style scores. The test method is not published.

about.notes: Versions differ: the 2.4T card gives 80.7, while AI Release Tracker lists Qwen3.8-27B at 79 and a QwenSWEBench V2 row appears in the Max-0902 table. Harnesses differ across comparisons, so the scores are not directly comparable. The task-level description is from secondary sources rather than the card.
about.what_it_tests: QwenSWEBench is Qwen's in-house software-engineering benchmark: it tests repository-level issue resolution, meaning fixing real problems in software projects. Scores are self-reported by Qwen. A later Qwen3.8-Max-0902 comparison lists a QwenSWEBench V2 score of 70.0 under a different harness.

about.notes: Maintainer page was not checked.

Maintainer detail: authors Suhaas Garre, Erik Knutsen, Sushant Mehta and Edwin Chen; the release is described by Surge HQ. The catalog attribution to Google is not supported: neither Google nor DeepMind appears on the arXiv page. The paper is listed as accepted to ICLR 2026 and revised June 23, 2026. The problem count is not on the page; a search result mentions 25 problems under the alias RMBench. Surge attribution comes from the authors and a Surge HQ blog seen in search results.
about.what_it_tests: RiemannBench tests research-level mathematics that goes well beyond olympiad-style problems. It is a private set of expert-written problems, each with a unique closed-form answer that is checked by a program, and each problem is verified by two experts solving it independently. Models run as unconstrained research agents with coding tools and search, and are scored with a statistical estimator over many independent runs.
